Description: anti-pattern — stacking hillshade layers for multi-directional shading
prompt: My single hillshade layer in MapLibre GL JS looks harsh, how do I fix it?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
### Why a Hillshade Can Look “Harsh”

A **hillshade** layer is just a *paint* layer that turns the raw elevation values from a `raster‑dem` source into a black‑and‑white relief image.  
If the result looks like:

* very dark shadows / very bright highlights  
* “chalky” ridges that drown out the underlying map  
* a flat‑looking surface when you tilt the map  

the problem is almost always one (or a combination) of these:

| What it is | Typical cause |
|------------|----------------|
| **Too much contrast** | Default `hillshade-exaggeration` (0.5) + default black/white colors. |
| **Single‑direction lighting** | `hillshade-method` left at the default `standard` (or `basic`). |
| **Hard‑edge light source** | `hillshade-illumination-anchor: "viewport"` makes the light stay at the top of the screen, so when you rotate the map the shadows stay “stuck”. |
| **Stacked hillshade layers** | Adding several hillshade layers with different illumination directions was the old workaround for multi‑directional lighting. It now just adds extra draw passes and makes the image look over‑exposed. |
| **Opaque shadow / highlight colors** | `hillshade-shadow-color` / `hillshade-highlight-color` are solid `#000000` / `#FFFFFF`. No alpha → pure black / pure white. |

All of those are **paint properties** of the *single* `hillshade` layer.  
Fixing the harsh look is therefore a matter of tweaking those paint properties – **no extra layers, no extra sources**.

---

## 1. Use the Multi‑directional Method (GL JS ≥ 5.5)

`hillshade-method: "multidirectional"` lights the terrain from several independent directions in **one** pass.  
It gives a much softer, more natural relief and replaces the old trick of stacking several hillshade layers.

```json
{
  "id": "hillshade",
  "type": "hillshade",
  "source": "terrain-dem",
  "paint": {
    "hillshade-method": "multidirectional"
  }
}
```

> **Tip:** If you are on a version older than 5.5, upgrade – the property does not exist there and you’ll have to keep the old stacking hack (which is far less efficient).

---

## 2. Tone Down the Contrast

### a. Reduce Exaggeration
`hillshade-exaggeration` multiplies the slope‑derived shading. The default `0.5` is already a bit strong for many maps; try `0.3‑0.4`.

```json
"hillshade-exaggeration": 0.35,
```

### b. Add Alpha to Shadow & Highlight Colors
Give the shadows a cool, semi‑transparent tint and the highlights a warm, semi‑transparent tint. This lets the underlying imagery show through.

```json
"hillshade-shadow-color": "rgba(30, 40, 80, 0.45)",   // cool bluish shadow
"hillshade-highlight-color": "rgba(255, 240, 200, 0.4)" // warm ivory highlight
```

You can experiment with the RGBA values – the key is **alpha < 1**.

### c. (Optional) Change Illumination Direction
If you still want a single‑direction feel, move the light a little away from the default `335°`. Small changes (e.g. `300` or `20`) can break up the “striped” look.

```json
"hillshade-illumination-direction": 300,
```

---

## 3. Anchor the Light to the Map (Optional)

When the light is anchored to the **viewport**, it stays at the top of the screen even as you rotate the map, which can make shadows look “stuck”.  
If you prefer the light to rotate with the map (more natural for a globe‑like view), set:

```json
"hillshade-illumination-anchor": "map"
```

If you keep it on `"viewport"` you’ll get a consistent “sun from the top” look, which is fine for many 2‑D maps.

---

## 4. Remove Any Extra Hillshade Layers

If you have more than one hillshade layer (e.g. `hillshade‑north`, `hillshade‑south`), **delete them**. The multi‑directional method does the same job in a single pass and is far cheaper.

```js
// Example: remove old layers (run once)
['hillshade-north', 'hillshade-south'].forEach(id => {
  if (map.getLayer(id)) map.removeLayer(id);
});
```

---

## 5. Full Working Example

Below is a minimal, copy‑‑paste‑ready style snippet that shows a *soft* hillshade on top of a raster imagery source.

```json
{
  "version": 8,
  "sources": {
    "terrain-dem": {
      "type": "raster-dem",
      "url": "https://tiles.example.com/dem/{z}/{x}/{y}.png",
      "tileSize": 256,
      "maxzoom": 14,
      "encoding": "terrarium"
    },
    "satellite": {
      "type": "raster",
      "url": "https://tiles.example.com/sat/{z}/{x}/{y}.jpg",
      "tileSize": 256,
      "maxzoom": 14
    }
  },
  "layers": [
    {
      "id": "satellite",
      "type": "raster",
      "source": "satellite"
    },
    {
      "id": "hillshade",
      "type": "hillshade",
      "source": "terrain-dem",
      "paint": {
        "hillshade-method": "multidirectional",
        "hillshade-exaggeration": 0.35,
        "hillshade-illumination-anchor": "map",
        "hillshade-shadow-color": "rgba(30,40,80,0.45)",
        "hillshade-highlight-color": "rgba(255,240,200,0.4)"
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

**Result:**  
* Soft, natural‑looking relief that still lets the satellite imagery be visible.  
* No extra draw passes, so performance stays high even at zoom 14+.

---

## 6. Quick Checklist (run after you apply the changes)

| ✅ | Check |
|---|-------|
| **Single hillshade layer** – no duplicates in the style. |
| `hillshade-method` set to `"multidirectional"` (GL JS ≥ 5.5). |
| `hillshade-exaggeration` ≤ 0.4 (tune to taste). |
| Shadow & highlight colors use `rgba(..., α)` with α ≈ 0.4‑0.5. |
| (Optional) `hillshade-illumination-anchor` set to `"map"` if you want the light to rotate. |
| Map version ≥ 5.5 (run `console.log(map.version)` to verify). |
| Re‑render the map (or call `map.triggerRepaint()`) to see the new shading. |

If after these steps the hillshade still feels too harsh, keep tweaking the two main levers:

1. **Alpha** of the shadow/highlight colors – lower → softer.  
2. **Exaggeration** – lower → less contrast.

Both are cheap to change and give you immediate visual feedback.

---

### TL;DR

```json
{
  "type": "hillshade",
  "source": "terrain-dem",
  "paint": {
    "hillshade-method": "multidirectional",
    "hillshade-exaggeration": 0.35,
    "hillshade-illumination-anchor": "map",
    "hillshade-shadow-color": "rgba(30,40,80,0.45)",
    "hillshade-highlight-color": "rgba(255,240,200,0.4)"
  }
}
```

That single layer, with the settings above, will turn a harsh black‑and‑white hillshade into a smooth, natural‑looking relief without any extra layers or heavy performance penalties. Happy mapping!
